title: What's Actually Inside a Black Box?

scenes.text: Every plane that has ever crashed left one survivor. It is not a person.
That survivor is me. I am the flight recorder. I sit in the tail, I listen to everything, and I am built to walk out of the one moment nobody else does.
scenes.cap: I'm the one who walks out.

scenes.text: People call me a black box. I have never been black. I am, and always have been, bright orange.

I can survive being slammed into the ground at three thousand four hundred times the force of gravity. Then set on fire at eleven hundred degrees Celsius. Then sunk under three kilometres of ocean for two years.
And when investigators finally open me up, the tiny board inside will tell them exactly how hundreds of people died — down to the last second.
So what is actually inside me? Who built the first one? And why can a fist-sized box survive a crash that a two hundred tonne aircraft cannot?
This is the story of the machine that outlives the disaster.
What's actually inside a black box.
Chapter one. The man they told to stop.

In nineteen thirty-four, a de Havilland airliner called the Miss Hobart fell into Bass Strait, off the coast of Australia. Eleven people died. The wreck was never found. The cause was never determined.
On board was a minister named Hubert Warren. He left behind a nine-year-old son, and one last gift — a small crystal radio set.
scenes.cap: A radio set, and a question.

scenes.text: That boy, David Warren, grew up to become a fuel scientist. And decades later he sat on the panel investigating the world's first jetliner, the de Havilland Comet, as it fell out of the sky again and again with no explanation.
Warren had a simple, radical thought. What if the cockpit could remember its own final minutes? What if the plane could testify?
scenes.query: David Warren flight memory unit prototype
scenes.cap: What if the plane could testify?

scenes.text: By nineteen fifty-six he had built it — the A R L Flight Memory Unit. It stored four hours of cockpit voices and instrument readings on a loop of fine steel wire.
scenes.query: ARL flight memory unit prototype Australia

scenes.text: Australia's response? The air force said it would yield, quote, more expletives than explanations. Civil aviation said it had little immediate use. Pilots feared being spied on. He was told to get back to fuel research.
It took a visitor from Britain to see it. In nineteen fifty-eight a British official watched a demonstration, understood instantly, and flew Warren to London to show it off. The idea finally caught.

Ironically, Australia became the first country on Earth to make cockpit voice recorders mandatory, in nineteen sixty. The United States followed with data recorders, then voice recorders through the mid nineteen sixties. The witness was now the law.
scenes.query: aviation regulation cockpit voice recorder history

scenes.text: He lost his father to a crash with no answers, and spent his life making sure no family ever had to hear those words again — cause, unknown. When David Warren died, his coffin was labelled: flight recorder inventor. Do not open.
Chapter two. Why orange is called black.
Here is the first myth, and it's about my own name. I am painted in a colour officially called international orange, so searchers can spot me in wreckage, in mud, on the sea floor.
scenes.query: orange flight recorder in wreckage debris

scenes.text: So why black box? Nobody can prove it. The best-documented answer is the least dramatic. In World War Two, British crews called the secret electronic units in their aircraft black boxes. The phrase was already slang for a mysterious device you judge only by what goes in and what comes out.
scenes.query: World War 2 aircraft radio radar equipment

scenes.text: You'll hear it was named because fire turns it black. That one is folklore. The name existed long before anyone filmed a charred recorder. Orange came first. Black was just what engineers called a box they couldn't see inside.
scenes.query: burned charred flight recorder fire damage
scenes.cap: The soot story is a myth.

scenes.text: Chapter three. Open me up.
Now the part you came for. What is actually inside. And the surprise is how little of me actually matters.

Most of my body is just electronics that do the recording in flight. In a crash, all of that is allowed to die. Only one part has to survive — this. The crash survivable memory unit. Everything else is packaging.
The outer wall is stainless steel or titanium, about a quarter of an inch thick. That's the skin that takes the impact and the crush.

Inside that is a block of dry silica thermal insulation — a full inch of it. That's the layer that lets me sit in an eleven hundred degree fire for an hour while the memory in the middle stays cool enough to survive.

And at the very centre, wrapped in all that armour, is the only thing that actually matters. A small stack of solid-state memory chips. No moving parts. Smaller than your hand. That is the real black box. The rest is a suit of armour built around it.
How tough is that armour, exactly? These are the certified numbers I have to pass before I'm allowed to fly.
Impact. Fired into a target at three thousand four hundred times the force of gravity, for six and a half thousandths of a second. That's like hitting a wall at hundreds of miles an hour.
Fire. Eleven hundred degrees Celsius for a full hour. Then a slow burn — two hundred and sixty degrees for ten hours — in case I'm buried in smouldering wreckage.
scenes.query: flight recorder fire furnace test flames

scenes.text: Crush. Five thousand pounds of static force on every axis. Puncture. A five hundred pound weight dropped onto a steel spike aimed straight at my heart. Pressure. Held at the equivalent of twenty thousand feet underwater.
And then, after all of that, I have to be soaked in seawater for thirty days and still give up every byte. That is what survivable means. Not indestructible. Survivable.
So here's the obvious question everyone asks. If this little box survives anything — why not build the whole plane out of it? Hold that thought. It's coming up, and the answer is beautiful.
Chapter four. What I actually hear.
There are really two of me on every airliner. The first is the cockpit voice recorder. It listens.
A microphone in the cockpit ceiling picks up everything — the pilots' words, the switches, the alarms, the engines, even the tone of a voice starting to break. Plus a channel for each crew member.

Older recorders kept only the last thirty minutes. Then two hours. New aircraft in Europe now keep a full twenty-five hours, and the United States is finally adopting the same. It runs on a loop, always erasing the oldest audio — which matters more than you'd think.
The second recorder is the flight data recorder. It doesn't listen. It knows.

The earliest ones tracked five things. Then eleven. Today I'm required to record at least eighty-eight parameters — and modern jets log well over a thousand: altitude, airspeed, every control input, every engine reading, many times a second, for twenty-five hours.
scenes.query: flight data recorder parameters graph readout

scenes.text: And here's a detail most people miss. Both of us live back here — in the tail. Not because it's convenient. Because in most crashes the tail is the last part to hit, and the furthest from the fuel and the fire. Where I sit is a survival decision.
Chapter five. How to find a box on the sea floor.
But surviving is useless if nobody can find me. So when I touch water, something wakes up.
A beacon on my side starts to ping — a sound pulse at thirty-seven point five kilohertz, once every second. It's a heartbeat, calling out from the dark, saying: I'm down here.
For decades that heartbeat lasted just thirty days. And that number nearly cost the world its most famous mystery.

In two thousand fourteen, a Boeing seven seven seven — Malaysia Airlines flight M H three seventy — vanished. Search teams didn't know where to look until the days were already burning down. My beacons likely fell silent before anyone arrived. The recorders have never been found.
scenes.query: MH370 ocean search aircraft Indian Ocean

scenes.text: So the rules changed. Now that beacon has to last ninety days, not thirty. And large aircraft carry a second, low-frequency beacon that can be heard from far, far further away. M H three seventy rewrote my design.
Chapter six. The two-year recovery.
Let me show you what it looks like when it works. Air France four forty-seven. Twenty oh nine. An Airbus stalled into the Atlantic in the dead of night. Two hundred and twenty-eight people lost.
My beacons died in thirty days. It took nearly two years, deep-tow sonar and robot submarines, to find the debris field — thirteen thousand feet down. Almost four kilometres of black water.
scenes.query: deep sea ROV submarine wreck search

scenes.text: In twenty eleven they lifted the memory modules from the sea bed. Two years of pressure and salt water — and every byte was intact. Over a single weekend, investigators read the entire final two hours. The stall. The confusion. The truth.
scenes.query: recovered flight recorder ship deck recovery

scenes.text: That is the whole point of me. Not to prevent the crash. To make sure it is never a mystery. To make sure it never happens the same way twice.
But what happens when I come back burned, shattered, or soaked? That's where the real magic is — in the lab.

A sea-recovered board is never allowed to dry out. Drying crystallises the salt and eats the circuits. So technicians keep it wet, then rinse it in pure, clean water to wash the salt away before they dare apply power.

And if my own electronics are destroyed but the memory chips are alive, they use a trick called the golden chassis. They lift the surviving chips out of the wreck and drop them into a pristine, identical recorder in the lab — and read them as if nothing ever happened.
scenes.query: circuit board chip memory extraction laboratory

scenes.text: Chapter seven. Everything you think you know.
Time to open the ones you've heard a hundred times, and grade them. And I get to be the judge.

Myth one. Why not build the whole plane out of black box material? Here's the beautiful answer. I survive because I'm small. My armour weighs a few kilos on a two hundred tonne aircraft — nothing. Scale that armour up to an entire fuselage and the plane is too heavy to ever leave the ground. A plane has to be light enough to fly. I get to be heavy because I'm tiny. Verdict: physics says no.

Myth two. Black boxes are indestructible. False — and I'd never claim otherwise. On September eleventh, the two recorders in the towers were never recovered. Some crashes exceed even my limits. I am crash survivable. That is a promise, not a boast. Verdict: false.

Myth three. They record video of the cockpit. Today — no. I capture audio and data only. Investigators have pushed for cockpit cameras for over a decade, and pilots' unions have fought it just as hard, over privacy. So for now, I listen. I don't watch. Verdict: false, but the fight isn't over.

Myth four. Someone is listening to you the whole flight. No one is. I record onto a loop that erases itself, and no human ever hears it — unless there's an accident. In many countries the law forbids that audio from being used to punish a crew, or from ever being made public. I am a witness, not a spy. Verdict: false.
Chapter eight. The recorder that ejects itself.
So what happens to me next? Because M H three seventy proved that sometimes, being tough isn't enough. Sometimes you have to be found — fast.

The first answer already flies on military jets and now on some airliners, like the Airbus A three fifty. A deployable recorder. In a crash it's fired clear of the tail — and because it floats, it rides on the surface instead of sinking four kilometres down.

The second answer is to never lose the data at all — stream it live to the ground, a black box in the cloud. The problem is brutal volume and cost, so for now it's used only in bursts, triggered when something goes wrong.
scenes.cap: A black box in the cloud.

scenes.text: And after M H three seventy, the world built a global tracking rule called GADSS. An aircraft in distress must now report its position at least once a minute — automatically, with no way for anyone on board to switch it off.

So that's me. A fist of memory, wrapped in armour, sitting in the tail — waiting for the worst day, so that day is never wasted. I am the promise that the truth survives, even when nothing else does. I am the only witness that walks out of every crash.

If you want to see everything I remember put to the test — watch the deadliest crash in history, where two of us on the ground held the answer. Or the one flight that beat me: M H three seventy, the Boeing seven seven seven that vanished from every radar on Earth.
I'm the black box. Subscribe to Black Box Breakdown — and next time, we'll open the ones that solved the impossible.
